title: I wrote 0 lines of code for my real-time PvP card battler: here's my Claude Code + Godot workflow
author: guillermosan
selftext:
Hi all,

I'm the solo developer of Cardume, and it was created using a 100% AI workflow, as in, I wrote 0 lines of code.

I did write this post myself.

As context: I've worked as a web developer half of my career, and I toyed with gaming projects but never had the intention to create a full game. I do have a folder full of old prototypes and half-baked ideas, mainly using Phaser and Godot.

At around Nov 2025, with Opus 4.5, I, like many in the industry, realized that AI-assisted coding was here to stay and went all-in on it in my day-to-day work processes with great results.

When I tested similar workflows using Godot and Claude Code, I was hooked. I could explore ideas and create complex systems FAST. Let me describe what is working for me.

**The important pieces of the setup:**

**Claude Code:** I've tried several models and harnesses; nothing compares to CC imho. Its only weak spot is image generation (it can't). Cardume uses basic vector shapes and lots of shaders as the palette, so I'm not bothered by that. I know people are completing their tasks using Codex too. The main takeaway is: **use a CLI coding assistant, not a chat app.**

**Linux:** Claude Code with full access to a Linux system is like giving it a workshop full of power tools. You can't replicate that in Windows. If CC needs a tool, it's an apt install away. I'm talking about video encoders, sound processing, graphical generation tools, the whole Linux command-line toolkit. Since it's a very bad idea to let AI loose with access to your important stuff (files and web browsing), it's a must to have a secure environment only for it. I use a virtual machine where CC has sudo and can do whatever it wants.

**Godot:** Everything you can do in the Godot editor can be done in code, meaning CC has access to 100% of the functionality. Not only that, CC has access to Godot source code; it can dive really deep into how things work. Ironically, I do not open the Godot editor at all.

**Git and CI:** This might seem obvious, but using git and CI (I use Gitea) is paramount, not only for organizing yourself, but because it provides Claude Code with a backbone. It can also be an automation layer. For example, you could have a CI job so that when any untranslated string is merged to main, an agent automatically picks up the task, does its job, and produces a PR. This is also important for TESTS. I know having tests is not something most game developers care about, but having tests is important for coding assistants. It keeps them on rails instead of reinventing solutions in different ways. Cardume has around 300 tests currently.

**The workflow:**

As said before, I don't use the Godot editor at all. I do write long and detailed prompts, but most importantly, **I ask for tools!** Cardume's iris UI was created using a custom shader panel with 15 knobs, and the arena has a panel with more than 50 knobs, from lighting to shaders to simulation. Most things I need to tweak end up in a set of knobs, or a throwaway environment or probe. I don't go "make this a bit brighter", but "wire brightness value in the panel".

Same with balance: I have benchmark tools and bot-vs-bot pipelines. When I change a card, there is a balance calculation process that can take hours. You are not asking CC to balance the game; instead, you create a tool to run thousands of games to balance with numbers.

**The strengths:**

Thanks to CC I've been able to do stuff beyond my capabilities. I don't know Rust, but my game is using a multithreaded deterministic kernel to enable fast multiplayer and thousands of simulated cells. I wouldn't dare to write cryptography, but my game is using signature chaining to prevent cheating. Most other things I could do before took many hours of reading and learning new APIs; now they are almost instant. Wire up Steam P2P? A prompt instead of days of new API and documentation digging. For me this is a freeing experience and I can only say positive things about it. Thanks to this dynamic I am going to ship my first commercial videogame. Even if it flops, I'm satisfied. For reference, Cardume's first commit was June 8th, 1304 commits since then. I plan to release before the year ends. Demo incoming for Next Fest.

**The weak parts:**

AI is bad at designing fun, deep, involved mechanics. It's also bad at art in general. While it can do small things here and there, it misses the big picture. You really need to have a clear idea and intention, artful and interesting, or "slop" will manifest. Both visually and mechanically. Cardume is my first game, and I've been learning along the way. While I spent a lot of time making it mechanically interesting and fun, in my next game I will make sure to have a more art-focused approach instead of the high-tech route this process led me down with Cardume.

Happy to answer any further questions about my workflow! And if you are curious about it, Cardume is in open playtest. Come try it, would love to have your feedback.

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/4912940/Cardume/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4912940/Cardume/)
